thread.title: Apple Shines, but Business Is Still Dreary in Smartphones

author: Tiernan Ray
title: Apple Shines, but Business Is Still Dreary in Smartphones
text:
By Tiernan Ray Updated May 2, 2018 3:39 p.m. ET Apple ’s ( AAPL ) stock is up $8.53, or 5%, at $177.63, steadily adding to gains, after its iPhone sales for the March quarter, reported yesterday afternoon , were not as bad as people expected, at 52.2 million units, versus some expectations as low as 49 million units.
But while that’s very good for Apple investors, it doesn’t mean the smartphone market is out of the woods.
Shipments for the entire industry dropped between 2% and 3% last quarter, depending on whose numbers you use.
China, in particular, continues to be weak , following a rough December quarter, with sales of smartphones there dropping in the March quarter by nearly 30% according to data released by China’s Ministry of Industry and Information.
The problem, according to industry observers, continues to be one of high-priced phones — such as the iPhone X — crimping people’s enthusiasm to trade in what they’ve got.
Strategy Analytics pegs the quarter’s total phone sales at 345 million units, a drop of 2%, and the firm’s Linda Sui places blame on "longer replacement rates, diminishing carrier subsidies, and a lack of new hardware design innovation.”
That’s despite the fact that Apple did well with the iPhone X, by the firm’s reckoning. It captured 15.1% market share, up from 14.4% a year earlier, slightly shaving Samsung Electronic ’s ( 005930KS ) first-place share, from 22.7% a year earlier to 22.6% last quarter.
Analyst Sui observed that the iPhone X is "proving relatively popular in some markets like China and the US, while there remains scope for additional expansion in emerging regions such as India and Africa.” Apple’s sales of all its products in China was up a nice 21% last quarter.
IDC pegs the decline last quarter at 2.9% , with a total of 334.3 million units sold by the industry. (Aside from Apple, no vendor reports their own unit shipments , hence, numbers are compiled as an estimate by IDC and Strategy Analytics and other analysts.)
While some consumers are “trading up to more premium devices,” believes IDC, in the words of analyst Anthony Scarsella, “despite new flagships from the likes of Samsung and Huawei, along with the first full quarter of iPhone X shipments, consumers looked unwilling to shell out big money for the latest and greatest devices on the market."
In fact, the best-performing companies last quarter were not the two giants, Apple and Samsung, but rather China’s two most prominent privately held companies, Huawei , and Xiaomi , according to Strategy Analytics.
Huawei’s unit sales rose to 11.4% share of the industry total, for a third place showing, up from 9.8% a year earlier. And Xiaomi jumped from 3.6% to 3.8%.
Units such as the “ Honor 7X ” helped Huawei deliver what the firm calls a “strong” shipment growth rate of 14%.
Xiaomi jumped ahead of another Chinese competitor, Oppo , thanks to its expansion — “like wildfire,” says Strategy Analytics — across various parts of Asia, especially India .
When will the pain end? Not soon. Chip analysts Joseph Moore and Craig Hettenbach , who cover chip makers whose wares go into smartphones, including Qorvo ( QRVO ) and Broadcom ( AVGO ), wrote on Monday that "we don't expect smartphone-exposed stocks to catch any sustained bid, even after the bad news gets out.”
Tune in this afternoon for the earnings report of Qorvo, which may bring extra tidbits.
